claims.text: Removing elements from equiatomic Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni changes local chemical interactions.
Local chemical interactions control lattice distortion, stacking-fault energy, and the propensity for dislocation-triggered FCC-to-HCP transformation.
Eliminating Mn reduces magnetic frustration relative to Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni.
Reduced magnetic frustration lowers the energetic barrier for localized FCC-to-HCP transformation at stacking faults and twin boundaries.
Changes in lattice conditions and transformation capacity alter dislocation mobility, work hardening, strength, and ductility.
The quinary alloy and the selected equiatomic ternary or quaternary subsets are single-phase FCC after identical thermomechanical processing.
A controlled comparison can be made by removing one or two elements while retaining an FCC initial structure and using identical processing.
Identical processing can ensure comparable grain size, defect density, and phase stability across the alloy variants.
Stacking-fault energy and local lattice distortion regulate dislocation slip.
Nanoscale HCP regions can occur in nominally FCC CrCoNi.
The relevant nanoscale HCP regions emerge during deformation at defect sites.
Removing Mn changes atomic-size, electronic, and magnetic interactions and reduces both lattice distortion and magnetic frustration.
Mn-free reduced-element alloys have a greater likelihood of deformation-induced FCC-to-HCP transformation than Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni.
Nanoscale HCP regions obstruct dislocation motion, enhance strain hardening, and modify yield behavior.
Relative to the quinary baseline, reduced-element alloys will show altered yield strength and work-hardening behavior.

A higher localized HCP fraction in reduced-element alloys will correlate with enhanced strain hardening and ductility when transformation strengthening dominates over the loss of lattice-distortion strengthening.
The occurrence of minority HCP in CrCoNi is sensitive to processing conditions, including cooling history.

The proposed mechanism is restricted to initially FCC, microstructurally comparable alloys tested at controlled temperature and strain rate and may fail when additional phases or substantial heterogeneity are present.
The net mechanical response depends on the competition between reduced lattice-distortion strengthening and transformation-enabled strain hardening.
Failure to observe a higher deformation-induced HCP fraction, systematic mechanical divergence, or mediator–property correlation in the reduced-element alloys would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The conditions state that processing should ensure comparable phase stability across variants, whereas the mechanism and prediction require the reduced-element alloys to have a systematically greater FCC-to-HCP transformation propensity. Comparable initial phases would be consistent, but comparable phase stability is not.
